elements.text: Relaxational Behavior of Poly(4-tetrahydropyranyl) Methacrylate

ABSTRACT: Complex permittivity ofpoly(4-tetrahydropyranyl methacrylate) (P4THPMA) was measured by dielectric spectroscopy. The spectra obtained show several relaxation processes labeled as d, c, b, and a in increasing order oftemperature. These processes have been characterized and assigned to specific molecular motions. Comparison of the dielectric activity obtained for P4THPMAwith those reported for poly(1,3-dioxan-5-yl-methacrylate) (PDMA) and poly(cyclohexyl methacrylate) (PCHMA) was performed. In fact, these three polymers have similar chemical structures with aliphatic rings in the ester residue. However, significant differences between the dielectric behavior of these polymers have been observed. In addition, complementary molecular mechanic (MM) calculations have been carried out. The energy barriers obtained by these calculations lead to energy barriers which are in relatively good agreement with those derived from the dielectric measurement by means Arrhenius plots. Keywords: dielectric relaxation processes; molecular mechanic calculations; poly(oxocyclohexyl methacrylate)s
INTRODUCTION

Although molecular mobility is severely restricted below the glass transition temperature, the dynamic glass transition (main transition or, conventionally a-relaxation) in polymers is usually accompanied by subglass secondary relaxations (b, c, d. . .-relaxations.). The glass transition at low temperatures is assumed to be caused by the cooperative motion of many particles, while the secondary relaxations have a more localized molecular origin. The number of these secondary relaxations usually depends on the nature of the side chain. Thus, polymers with side chains with a large number of degrees of freedom are susceptible to undergo several molecular motions, which are visualized as a large number of secondary relaxation processes. In particular, polymers with cyclohexyl side groups are characterized for displaying considerable dielectric and mechanical activity in the glassy state.<sup>1–9</sup> Therefore, this type of polymers is especially suitable to study the lateral chain dynamics above and below the glass transition temperature. It should be also interesting to study how the modifications in the side group of poly(cyclohexyl methacrylate) (PCHMA)<sup>2</sup> affects the dielectric response. In particular, the substitution of a carbon by oxygen in the cyclohexyl ring should affect the relaxational behavior of the resulting polymer. In an earlier work, the dielectric and mechanical relaxations of poly(1,3-dioxan-5-yl-methacrylate) (PDMA)<sup>10</sup> has been investigated and it has been found that this polymer shows a variety of absorptions due to the versatility of its structural moiety.

elements.text: The aim of the present work is to analyze the response of poly(4-tetrahydropyranyl) methacrylate (P4THPMA) to dynamic electric fields in both the glassy state and in the glass–rubber transition zone. To study the effect of structural modifications in the cyclohexyl ring at the end of the side chain, these results are compared with those reported for PDMA and PCHMA. A schematic representation of the repeating unit of P4THPMA, PDMA, and PCHMA is shown in Figure 1.

Molecular mechanics (MM) is a powerful tool for analyzing the molecular motions causing secondary relaxations.<sup>11,12</sup> For this reason, and to check the energy barriers associated with specific molecular motions that are responsible for the lower temperature relaxation processes, conformational calculations have been carried out. A comparison is made between the energy barrier values obtained by Arrhenius diagram (log s as a function of 1/T, where $\omega _ { \mathrm { m a x } } = 1 / \tau$is the frequency of the maximum loss factor) and those obtained by MM.
EXPERIMENTAL
Monomer and Polymer Preparation

4-Tetrahydropyranyl methacrylate was prepared by reaction of methacryloyl chloride with 4-tetrahydropyranyl alcohol in toluene solutions and pyridine at reflux temperature for 30 h according to the technique described by Burtle and Turek.<sup>13</sup> Purification was achieved by distillation under vacuum. Monomer was polymerized in toluene solutions under vacuum in sealed tubes, in presence of $\alpha , \alpha ^ { \prime } \cdot$-azobisisobutyronitrile (AIBN) $5 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 }$to $1 0 ^ { - 2 } \ \mathrm { ~ ( w / w ) }$% as previously reported.<sup>14</sup> Polymer was fractionated by solubility in toluene/methanol as solvent–nonsolvent pair. Three fractions were obtained and the fraction of the middle was selected for the present study.

The glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$of the pure polymer was measured with a Mettler 821 calorimetric system. Polymer sample was dried under reduced pressure in a vacuum oven prior to measurement. Dry nitrogen was used as purge gas and thermogram was measured in the range 308– 523 K at a scan rate of 20 $\mathrm { K } \mathrm { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$. The glass transition temperature obtained for the P4THPMA was 433 K.
Dielectric Measurements

Dielectric measurements were carried out by means of a Novocontrol Broad Band Dielectric Spectrometer made up of an Alpha analyzer to carry out measurement from $1 0 ^ { - 1 } ~ \mathrm { t o } ~ 1 0 ^ { 6 }$Hz and an Agilent 4991A RF analyzer to perform measurements from ${ 1 0 } ^ { 6 }$to ${ 1 0 } ^ { 8 }$Hz, both devices being coupled with a Quatro temperature controller. Isothermal measurements were carried out from 148 to 423 K in 5-K steps on a molded, disc-shaped (diameter of 20 and 10 mm, respectively) sample.
Simulation Methodology and Computational Details

MM calculations were performed using the force field method developed by Allinger and coworkers.<sup>15–18</sup> Other procedures, for example, ab initio molecular orbital calculations should also be useful for the same purpose, but in the present study a force field method has been used. The PC-
MODEL software<sup>19</sup> was employed to carry out the calculations. It is based on an empirical force field, called MMX that is derived from MM2(P).<sup>20</sup>
The use of the model compounds is advisable to simplify the calculations and the corresponding interpretations of the obtained results in a way similar to those of other authors.<sup>1,21–28</sup>

This empirical force field includes intermolecular as well as intramolecular contributions. The nonbonded energy function expresses interactions between atoms that are not bonded to each other. It is split into a van der Waals steric component and an electrostatic component, dealing with interactions between charges and dipoles. A Buckingham potential was used for this purpose. Parameterization of MMX has been carried out, assuming an artificial dielectric constant of 1.5.

The intramolecular energy function is split into a connectivity term, the bond stretching function and flexibility terms, the angle bending and the torsional functions, as well as cross-terms describing the coupling of stretch–bend, bend–bend, and torsional–stretch interactions that are taken into account. The Wilson $( E _ { \mathrm { O O P } } ,$our umbrella out-ofplane) term has also been included, but their contribution to the global energy was small in all cases.

The first step in the calculations is to establish an initial geometry. Exploration of the conformational characteristics of representative skeletal fragments of the polymers is therefore a prerequisite to model, adequately, larger fragments. The calculations of the theoretical energy requirements for a bond rotation were carried out with model compounds of one unit for each polymer, which simulate part of the polymer chain. The minimization was performed using a combination of steepest descent and Newton-Raphson meth-$\mathrm { 0 d s ^ { 2 9 } }$until the energy gradient falls below 0.0004 kJ mol-<sup>1</sup> A<sup>˚</sup> -<sup>1</sup> for each specific conformer.

Dielectric Measurements

At high temperatures and low frequencies, important conductivity contributions appear since the loss permittivity tends to increase continuously.

To analyze loss permittivity in the subglass zone in a more detailed way, it is convenient to fit the loss factor permittivity by means of usual empirical equations. A reliable model to represent the secondary relaxations in polymers is the symmetric Fuoss and Kirkwood equation (FK).<sup>30</sup> To split the two overlapped relaxations $( \gamma$and $\beta ) ,$addition of each one of these contributions to the relaxation spectrum have been assumed. According to this procedure, the following equation to represent the empirical data is proposed

The parameter m is related to the relaxation time distribution in such a way that the higher $m _ { : }$, the narrower the distribution is, being $m = 1$for Debye type relaxation. The function was determined from a multiple nonlinear regression analysis of the experimental data, allowing the three characterizing peak parameters $( \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { m a x } , i } ^ { \prime \prime } , \bar { m _ { i } } E _ { \mathrm { a } , i } \big / R , T _ { \mathrm { m a x } , i } )$to vary. Table 1 compiles the fitting parameters obtained, the corresponding values of $m _ { i } ,$and the strength of the two relaxations obtained from the relationship,<sup>31</sup> $\begin{array} { r } { \varepsilon _ { \mathrm { ~ } \mathrm { ~ m a x } , i } ^ { \prime \prime } = \frac { m _ { i } \cdot \Delta \varepsilon _ { i } } { 2 } } \end{array}$. The errors for each one of the fitting parameters show the quality of the fit. As an example, Figure 4 shows the c- and b-relaxations that result from the application of the multiple nonlinear regression analysis to the loss factor versus temperature at 10.3 Hz. The sum of the two calculated relaxations is very close to that in the experimental curve.

The evolutions of the frequency of the maxima show a linear dependency with the inverse temperature according to the expectations (see Fig. 3). The activation energies calculated from the Arrhenius plot for each process were $6 8 . 2 \pm 0 . 6 \mathrm { k J } \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 }$for $\beta -$relaxation and 48.0 6 0.3 kJ $\mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } }$for c-relaxation. These values are very close to those found for polymers structurally related to P4THPMA such as $\mathrm { P C H M A } , ^ { 2 }$PMCHMA,<sup>6</sup> poly(2chloro cyclohexyl methacrylate),<sup>9</sup> and PDMA<sup>10</sup> (70–82 and 41–50 kJ $\mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } } )$. The $m _ { \gamma }$and $m _ { \beta }$parameters do not show a noticeable dependence on the frequency. The low values obtained for this parameter, in the case of the b-relaxation, seem to be an indication of the distributed character of the process.

It is convenient to remember that the c-relaxation in polymers containing cyclohexyl groups was assigned to the change in the conformation chair-to inverse chair in the cyclohexyl group.<sup>1,2,6,9,10</sup> On the other hand, the b-relaxation in PMMA is attributed by several authors<sup>22,23</sup> to the partial rotation of the ester lateral group as a whole coupled with some type of motions of the main chain. By using 2D-NRM measurements, Spiess and coworkers 32 have concluded that for PMMA and PEMA, the unusual main chain mobility below $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$is coupled to the b-relaxation process, which involves $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$flips of the carboxyl side groups.

As usual, the relaxation strength ofthe subglass processes increases as the frequency decreases. The relaxation strength of c-relaxation in P4THPMA is close to the corresponding to PCHM $\mathbf { A } ^ { 2 } \left( \Delta \varepsilon _ { \gamma } \sim 0 . 0 5 \right)$and significantly lower than that of the corresponding to $\mathrm { P D M A } ^ { 1 0 } \left( \Delta \varepsilon _ { \gamma } \sim 0 . 9 \right)$

This phenomenon suggests that conductivity contributions are dominant over dipolar processes in this zone.

elements.text: Molecular Mechanics Study

Molecular simulation techniques allow us to provide an explanation of the molecular origin of the observed secondary relaxations. In this way, we will now make a tentative interpretation ofthe molecular origin of the observed secondary relaxations. To elucidate the specific motions responsible of the observed secondary relaxations, we have calculated and compared the conformational energy barriers with the activation energies obtained from dielectric measurements. The optimized geometry of the one-unit model compound of P4THPMA calculated by force field MMX is represented in Figure 5.

The activation energy obtained by dielectric measurements for d-process is 28 kJ mol-<sup>1</sup>. This value is close to that obtained for PCHMA.<sup>2</sup> Therefore, the molecular origin of both relaxation processes should be related. This relaxation is presented in cyclohexyl compounds at temperatures below the c-relaxation and, several authors<sup>1</sup> have related this relaxation to the motions of cyclohexyl group as a whole. To interpret the molecular motions responsible for d-transition, the calculations were confined to the rotation of the cyclohexyl ring around the O C bonds.

elements.text: Figure 6 shows the potential energy profiles obtained for the rotation of the O C bond. In this calculation the specified dihedral angle $( \phi _ { 1 } )$is constrained to certain desired values (in the range 1808 and 1808, step 58) and the remaining parts of the molecule are allowed to move freely to minimize the energy. An energy barrier of 31 kJ $\mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } }$was obtained. This value is close to that evaluated from dielectric measurements $( { \sim } 2 8 \mathrm { k J } \mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$

The following relaxation observed moving to higher temperatures, is designated as the c-process. According to our study recently reported in related polymers,<sup>7</sup> we start assuming that the observed c-relaxation is mainly associated with the barrier hindering the chair-to-chair interconversion of the cyclohexyl group. It is known that the chair-to-chair interconversion is a complex process produced by successive conformational changes within the molecule. When an isolated cyclohexyl ring undergoes internal rotations, the chair-to-chair transition in the cyclohexyl ring follows the sequence given by chair ? half-chair ? boat ? half-chair ? chair. The half-chair form is not stable because the hydrogen atoms at the foot are eclipsed with those on the adjacent carbons, and because of this fact, there is some angular strain. These angular strains occur because the molecule is nearly planar and are destabilized by torsional strain. When the cyclohexyl ring is bounded to the polymer chain, the motion is something different to that before mentioned. In this case, the motion that produces the transition from one chair form to another fixes the oxycarbonyl group to the main chain and therefore this group remains nearly in the same position above and after the chair-to-chair transition.

Table 3 summarizes the energetic contributions, the energy barrier and shows a scheme of the chair-to-chair transition. The energy barrier was calculated as the difference between the energy of the less favorable conformation (the half-chair) and the more stable conformation (chair). The energy barrier obtained with a simple model compound of one unit (46.1 kJ $\mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$is close to that evaluated by dielectric measurements (48.0 kJ mol-<sup>1</sup>). Thus, the MM calculations strongly support the idea of an intramolecular barrier for the crelaxation associated with the chair-to-chair interconversion of the cyclohexyl ring at the end of the side chain.

To have a better understanding of the effect of the presence of the oxygen in the cyclohexyl ring, we have carried out a comparative analysis of the last two processes (d and c), for P4THPMA and the two structurally related polymers, PCHMA and PDMA (see Fig. 1). Figure 6 shows the minimum static conformational energy (in kJ $\mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$as a function of the torsional angle of the lateral unit $( \phi _ { 1 } )$for the three polymers under study. Rotations show a specific energy profile, which depends on the local environment of each group. In all the cases, the shape of the obtained energy profiles is very similar, but the energy barriers are not the same. Their value is higher when the number of oxygen atoms in the cyclohexyl ring is lower: 34 (PCHMA), 31 (P4THPMA), and 27 (PDMA) kJ mol-<sup>1</sup>.

elements.text: The activation energy of the c-relaxation obtained from the Arrhenius plot (Fig. 3) is scarcely affected by the oxygen substitution in the ring. In fact, the activation energy for the c-process of the dioxo-derivatives (PDMA, 43.8 kJ mol-<sup>1</sup>) is close to that obtained for the hydrocarbon ring (PCHMA, 43.1 kJ $\mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$and, somewhat smaller than that evaluated for the mono-oxo-derivative (P4THPMA, 48.0 kJ $\mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$The main effect observed in the c-process refers to the height of the peaks. In fact, PDMA shows a c-peak about 10 times higher than that ofPCHMA and P4THPMA.

Table 4 summarizes the parameters used to explain the differences observed in the c-relaxation zone when one, two, or no carbon atoms of the cyclohexyl ring are substituted by oxygen atoms. The energy barriers derived by Force Field MMX (43 (PCHMA), 46 (P4THPMA), and 44 (PDMA) kJ $\mathrm { m o l } ^ { - 1 } )$are close to those obtained from dielectric relaxations measurements (43.1, 48, and 43.8 kJ $\mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } }$, respectively). On the other hand, an interpretation of the relaxation strength of the $\gamma { \mathrm { - p e a k } } ^ { 3 1 }$for the three polymers under study has been carried out in terms of strain energy (SE) values. SE is defined as the difference between the steric energy of the molecule and the steric energy if all the components of the molecule were in a strainfree environment. In PDMA, due to the small values of SE in the intermediate state (half-chair), in comparison with the other two polymers, a higher fraction of the cyclohexyl ring should be able to participate in the motion provoking the c-relaxation. In other words, the low height of the c-peak in P4THPMA and PCHMA in comparison with that of PDMA could be explained by the blocking of the motion of part of the rings due to the less stable intermediate state in chair-to-chair transition when one or no carbon in the cyclohexyl group is substituted by an oxygen atom.

Our calculation shows that the ratio of molecules involved with respect to PCHMA is near to unity for P4THPMA and 9 for PDMA. Thus, the number of dipolar entities that participate in the c-relaxation is about 10 times higher in the case of PDMA than for the other two polymers. This fact is in good agreement with the experimental data that show that the relaxation strength is larger for the PDMA than for the PCHMA and P4THPMA.

elements.text: It is remarkable that the main conclusion of the precedent analysis is based on the hypothesis than c-relaxation is mainly governed by intramolecular barriers. However, this is not the situation for the case of the $\beta \mathrm { - r e l a x a t i o n . }$. In fact it is well known, in light of the recent theories, that the b-relaxation can be due to the local motions in the main chain. In this case the b-relaxation can be considered as a precursor of the a-relaxation and is labeled a Johari–Goldstein (JG) relaxation.<sup>40,41</sup> When the $\beta \mathfrak { - }$relaxation is caused by partial rotation of the side chain as a whole, in combination with motions of the main chain, contributions to the barrier due to the main chain cannot be ruled out. Consequently, in this case the energy barriers opposed to the molecular motion, probably have inter- as well as intramolecular origin.<sup>41</sup>

For the b-relaxation, the activation energy obtained from dielectric analysis is close to that corresponding to PMMA, but the well-defined $\beta \mathfrak { - }$peak in PMMA is strongly depressed in P4THPMA (as in PCHMA) probably due to the effect of the bulky cyclohexyl group. As mentioned above, the b-relaxation in PMMA is attributed by several authors to the partial rotation of the ester lateral group as a whole coupled with some type of motions of the main chain.<sup>22,23,32</sup> According to these explanations, and taking into account the proximity of the ester group to the main chain, we have analyzed the energetic requirements by MM calculations using a three-unit model. By this way, it is possible to avoid the effect of the backbone on the rotation of the ester side group. In this threeunit model compound, we take into account the interactions between different side groups and presumably we should obtain more realistic results. Thus, the energy requirements for overall rotation $( \phi _ { 2 } \ : \mathrm { f r o m } - 1 8 0 ^ { \circ } \ : \mathrm { t o } + 1 8 0 ^ { \circ } )$of the side chain as a whole, for the model compound with three units was 58 kJ $\mathrm { m o l ^ { - 1 } }$. Nevertheless, two successive rotations $( - 1 8 0$to 5408) of the same bond have neither the same profile nor the same energetic requirement. In this way, this relaxation should involve motions not only of the side chain ester group but also local motions of the main chain, as mentioned for poly(methacrylate)s.<sup>1</sup> The contribution of various motions to this relaxation could explain the low value obtained for the m parameter in the Fuoss and Kirkwood equation (FK).

elements.text: CONCLUSIONS

At low temperatures a d-relaxation was found. This relaxation process is probably related to the rotation of the cyclohexyl ring around the $\mathrm { O - C }$bond. Our MM results confirm that the energy barrier associated with that the d-relaxation is strongly dependent on chemical structure, specifically on the presence or absence of oxygen atoms in the cyclohexyl ring.

The c-relaxation that was associated with the chair-to inverse chair interconversion does not change significantly in energy barrier values when carbon were changed by oxygen atoms; however the height of this relaxation increases when the carbon in position 4 of the ring is substituted by an oxygen atom. Figure 7(a,b) shows the effect of the substitution of one or two carbons by oxygen atoms in the cyclohexyl ring on the loss permittivity and electric modulus (M00), respectively.

Two procedures have been used to explain the low value of the height of the c-peak in P4THPMA and PCHMA in comparison with PDMA. The first one takes into account the strain energy (SE) values (kJ mol-<sup>1</sup>) of the intermediate in chair-to-chair transition (half-chair) in the three polymers PDMA (1.672) << P4THPMA (21.318) < PCHMA (37.620). According to this parameter, the number of relaxing species per volume unit should be larger in PDMA. The second takes into account the fact that the c-process is mainly intramolecular in origin. The OFK equation<sup>37</sup> together with the approach to the problem by Smith and $\mathrm { B o y d } ^ { 3 9 , \hat { 4 } 2 }$allow us to estimate the relative number of relaxing species per volume unit involved in the c-relaxation process which is larger in PDMA than in the case of the other two polymers.

On the other hand, it is noticeable that the $\gamma -$relaxation of P4THPMA, at a given frequency, is located at nearly 20 K above than that of PDMA and at approximately the same temperature of PCHMA.<sup>2</sup> This behavior suggests that the frequency factor in Arrhenius equation, which represents the frequency of the formation of relaxing conformations susceptible to crossing the barrier energies, is lower for PCHMA and P4THPMA (ln $f _ { \mathrm { { o } } } = 2 9 . 9 3 \pm 0 . 5 4 )$than for PDMA (ln $f _ { \mathrm { o } } = 3 0 . 7 2$6 0.05).

The b-relaxation is assigned to the rotation of the alkoxycarbonyl group coupled with short range motions of the main-chain. For P4THPMA the maximum is located nearly 40 K lower than for PDMA and PCHMA (see Fig. 7). In contrast to the two other polymers (PCHMA and PDMA), the $\beta \mathfrak { - }$relaxation of P4THPMA is enough separated from a-relaxation to be characterized in terms of an empirical equation. The broadening of the dielectric b-peak (low value of the $m _ { \beta }$parameter in FK equation) in the temperature domain could be due to an overlapping of a variety of local environments, controlled each one of them, with their corresponding energy barrier.

The a-relaxation is also affected by the different nature of the rings located in the side groups. Specifically, in the case of P4THPMA, this process is located ca. 40 K and 45 K above that of PDMA and PCHMA, respectively. In all polymers analyzed, important conductive processes are present at high temperatures. Clarification of this fact could be obtained by using the electric modulus formalism $( M ^ { * } = 1 / \mathrm { { g } ^ { * } ) }$(see [Fig. 7(b)]) Two processes at high temperature are observed for both PCHMA and P4THPMA. In both cases, these processes can be associated with the conductive effects and to the dipolar a-relaxation, respectively. At high temperature the curve corresponding to PDMA only shows a shoulder close to the maximum of the conductive peak. This suggests strong overlapping between the a-relaxation and the conductive processes for this polymer.
